opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is a really interesting question, and it's one where I think the answer is a little more subtle than people often assume. There's this very appealing picture that the brain has some kind of internal simulator, a little physics engine in your head, and when you make a decision you roll out different possibilities, see what happens, and pick the best one. And I think there's some truth to that. Clearly people can imagine things, they can think through consequences, they can plan.

But I'm skeptical that it looks like what we would call simulation in robotics or in model-based RL, where you predict every pixel or every state variable into the future. That's extremely expensive, and frankly it's not necessary for most decisions. What I suspect is going on is that the brain learns representations that are already shaped around what matters for acting. So when you "imagine" something, you're not rendering a full video of the future. You're predicting the parts that are relevant to your goals: will this work, will I reach the thing I want, what's the rough outcome.

From a machine learning perspective, that actually blurs the line between model-based and model-free methods. A value function, in a sense, is a kind of simulation. It's a compressed prediction about what will happen in the future if you behave a certain way. It just doesn't tell you the intermediate details. And I think a lot of what looks like deliberate simulation in people might really be something like that: learned predictions about future outcomes at the right level of abstraction, which you can sometimes chain together when you need to reason more carefully.

The other piece I'd emphasize is that whatever the brain is doing, it's trained on an enormous amount of real experience. The ability to imagine comes from having interacted with the world. You can mentally simulate pouring a cup of coffee because you've done things like that many times. So I don't think simulation replaces experience. It's more of a way to get more mileage out of experience you already have, recombining it to handle situations you haven't seen exactly before.

That's also why I think for building robots and intelligent systems, the lesson isn't necessarily "build a better simulator." It's more that you want systems that learn from real data and develop predictive representations that let them generalize and plan when needed. The simulation is something learned, not something hand-engineered, and it's shaped by the decisions the agent actually has to make.

r001.rationale: The response describes learned representations that predict relevant future outcomes, which can be chained to reason about possibilities not seen before.

r002.rationale: It mentions choosing the best option in an opening description of a popular picture, but does not clearly state that optimal decision making requires comparing whether one action produces a better outcome than another.

r003.rationale: It says decision-relevant predictions can be learned in abstract representations and explicitly rejects the need to build a better, hand-engineered simulator.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually a really interesting question, and I think the way I'd approach it is maybe a little bit different from how people in neuroscience would approach it, because I come at it from the perspective of building systems that have to make decisions.

So if you think about what simulation means in the context of decision-making, essentially what you're doing is you're using some kind of a model of the world to ask "what if" questions. What if I take this action, what will happen next, and will that be good or bad? And the appeal of that is obvious: if you have a good model, you can plan, you can anticipate consequences, you can avoid making mistakes that would otherwise be very costly in the real world.

But I think there's a subtlety here that gets lost a lot, which is that simulation is actually only one of several ways you could use experience to make decisions. The other way, which is sort of the classic reinforcement learning answer, is that you just learn from the outcomes directly. You try things, you see what happens, and you kind of cache the result, so next time you're in a similar situation you don't need to simulate anything, you just know what to do. And there's good reason to believe that the brain does a lot of both. The habitual, fast, intuitive kind of decision-making looks a lot like that cached, model-free thing, and then the slower, more deliberate reasoning looks more like you're rolling out a model in your head.

Now, the part that I find really interesting, and this is where I think the AI perspective is useful, is that these two things are not actually as separate as they might seem. Because where does the model come from? It comes from experience. And where does the cached knowledge come from? Also from experience. So in some sense, what you're really talking about is just different ways of compressing and reusing the same underlying data. A model is kind of a very general-purpose compression. It lets you answer lots of questions you haven't asked before. A cached value or a policy is a very specific compression. It only answers the question you were trained on, but it answers it fast.

And I think the right picture of what's going on in a brain, or in a really capable AI system, is not "it simulates" or "it doesn't simulate," but rather that it has a lot of flexibility in how much computation it spends at decision time. When the situation is familiar, you use the cheap answer. When the situation is novel, or the stakes are high, you spend more compute, and that compute often looks like simulation, like imagining outcomes.

One thing I'd also say, just to be a bit provocative, is that I don't think the simulation in the brain is anything like a physics simulator. It's not like you have a little model of the world that's faithful in every detail. It's a very abstract, very lossy thing, and it's lossy in a way that's shaped by what matters for your decisions. You simulate the things that are relevant to the outcome, and you ignore everything else. And honestly that's something we've struggled with a lot in robotics, because the natural thing to do is build a model that predicts everything, every pixel, every detail, and that turns out to be both very hard and not necessarily what you want. What you want is a model that's good at predicting the things you care about. And I suspect the brain figured that out a long time ago.

r001.rationale: The response describes using a model learned from experience to ask what-if questions and says deliberate reasoning can roll out that model in the brain.

r002.rationale: It discusses whether an action will be good or bad, but does not state that optimal decision making requires comparing the outcomes of alternative actions.

r003.rationale: It says cached knowledge can guide decisions without simulation, presenting simulation as one of several ways to use experience.

astra-6.text:
I think simulation is probably one of several mechanisms we use to make decisions. Sometimes you act almost reflexively, based on patterns you've learned from experience. Other times you seem to imagine the consequences of an action before taking it: if I do this, what might happen, and what would I do next?

In reinforcement learning, we'd call that second approach model-based planning. You have some internal model of how the world works, and you use it to evaluate possible actions. But that model doesn't have to produce a detailed, physically accurate movie. It might predict something much more abstract, like how someone will react to something you say.

The interesting question is when it's worth doing that computation. You can't deliberate about every muscle movement involved in picking up a cup. You want learned behaviors to handle the familiar parts, and you want to simulate when there's uncertainty or when the consequences matter. So my guess is that a lot of the sophistication lies in deciding what to think about, and at what level of abstraction. That's a useful perspective for building artificial systems, too, although I wouldn't take it as an established account of how the brain implements these things.

r001.rationale: It describes using an internal model to imagine what might happen after an action, which suggests evaluating counterfactuals through a learned model.

r002.rationale: It says the model can evaluate possible actions, but does not state that optimal decision making requires comparing whether one action would produce a better outcome than another.

r003.rationale: It says predictions can be abstract rather than a detailed, physically accurate movie, but does not say decision-relevant counterfactuals can be answered without an explicit simulator.

sol-6.1.text:
I think simulation is probably part of the story, but we should distinguish between having a model of what might happen and explicitly running that model forward to choose an action.

If I reach for a cup, I probably don't imagine every possible trajectory of my hand and then pick the best one. A lot of that behavior is learned and fairly automatic. But if the cup is precariously balanced, I might pause and think, “If I grab it this way, will I knock it over?” That's a situation where imagining an outcome could be useful.

In reinforcement learning, we often describe these as model-free and model-based approaches. The model-free approach learns which actions tend to work. The model-based approach predicts consequences and uses those predictions to make a decision. I suspect the brain uses some combination, although that distinction is cleaner in our algorithms than it necessarily is in biology.

And simulation can also help you learn, rather than just help you decide in the moment. You could imagine an outcome, use that to improve your policy, and then act without doing that computation again. So observing fast, seemingly automatic behavior doesn't necessarily tell you that a model wasn't involved in producing it.

r001.rationale: The response connects imagining outcomes with a model that predicts consequences, but it does not clearly say that the model is learned or that it evaluates counterfactuals.

r002.rationale: It says predictions can inform a decision, but does not state that optimal decision making requires comparing possible actions to determine which would produce a better outcome.

r003.rationale: It says automatic behavior does not rule out a model being involved, but does not explain that decision-relevant counterfactual questions can be answered without an explicit simulator.
